opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few bottlenecks, and they're not all on the modeling side.

The first one people usually point to is **recall and retrieval**. Linear attention compresses the whole history into a fixed-size state, so it's fundamentally lossy. Softmax attention keeps a KV cache that grows with the sequence, so it can look back and fetch an exact token. For tasks like associative recall, needle-in-a-haystack, or in-context copying, pure linear models still lag. A lot of recent work, like the delta rule, gating, and larger state expansions, is about using that fixed memory more cleverly: deciding what to overwrite instead of only accumulating. It helps a lot, but I don't think the gap is fully closed. That's why many production-oriented designs are hybrids that interleave a few softmax attention layers with mostly linear layers.

The second bottleneck is **hardware efficiency**. On paper linear attention is O(N), but people often found that naive implementations were slower than FlashAttention in wall-clock time at moderate sequence lengths. GPUs love big matrix multiplies, and a recurrent formulation isn't naturally tensor-core friendly. So a big part of what I've worked on is chunkwise parallel algorithms, where you do matmul-heavy computation inside chunks and pass a recurrent state between chunks. That made training competitive. But every new variant, especially ones with more expressive state transitions, needs its own careful kernel work, and that slows down iteration.

The third is **ecosystem and infrastructure**. Everything in the inference stack, including serving frameworks, paged KV caches, speculative decoding, and prefix caching, was built around the Transformer. Linear and hybrid models need different memory management and state handling. That engineering inertia is real. Even if a model is better in theory, a team has to justify rebuilding part of its stack.

Finally, there's an **evaluation and scaling-evidence** problem. Most linear-attention results come from academic-scale experiments, at a few billion parameters at most. Companies want to see that the advantages hold, and the weaknesses don't get worse, at frontier scale and on long-context agentic workloads. Generating that evidence is expensive, so there's a bit of a chicken-and-egg problem.

So if I had to summarize: the core scientific question is how to get a fixed-size state to be expressive enough for retrieval-heavy tasks, and the practical question is making these models first-class citizens in the hardware and software stack. I'm fairly optimistic, especially as long-context reasoning and agents make the cost of quadratic attention and huge KV caches more painful.

r001.rationale: The response lists infrastructure as one of several bottlenecks, but does not identify it as the main deployment bottleneck relative to algorithmic readiness.

r002.rationale: It discusses kernel work and hardware efficiency, but does not attribute Flash Linear Attention's kernel efficiency to Triton.

r003.rationale: It does not describe open-source model releases prompting inference-engine developers to add support.

r004.rationale: It says teams must justify rebuilding their stack, but does not explain that a better inference ecosystem lowers the deployment barrier for other companies.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest, Songlin Yang, drawing only on the conversation so far.

Thanks for having me. I'd say the bottleneck isn't really the math anymore. The attention-side algorithms exist, and we know how to make them fast on GPUs. The real friction is twofold.

First, there's the ecosystem problem. The entire inference stack, from serving frameworks to KV-cache management to speculative decoding to quantization, has been co-designed with softmax attention for years. Linear attention replaces the KV cache with a fixed-size recurrent state, which sounds great, but it means every one of those tools has to be rethought. Chunked prefill, prefix caching, continuous batching, all of it assumes you can index into a cache that grows with sequence length. So even when a linear model is competitive on quality, the surrounding infrastructure is immature, and that slows adoption more than any benchmark gap does.

Second, there's the question of what people actually trust at scale. Most of the evidence for linear attention comes from models in the one-to-several-billion range. When a lab is about to spend tens of millions of dollars on a run, they want to know the architecture won't fall over at seventy billion or several hundred billion parameters, especially on retrieval-heavy and long-context tasks where the fixed state is genuinely a constraint. That's why hybrids have become the practical answer: a few layers of full attention mixed with mostly linear layers gets you most of the efficiency while hedging the risk. I think the honest picture is that pure linear attention still has to earn trust at frontier scale, and the hybrid design space is where the near-term deployment will happen.

If I had to pick one thing I'd most like to see solved, it's better kernel and systems support so that people can try these architectures without rewriting their whole serving stack. Once the engineering cost drops, the research questions get answered much faster, because many more groups can run real experiments.

r001.rationale: The response says the main friction is the immature inference ecosystem, while attention algorithms already exist and can be made fast on GPUs.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Flash Linear Attention, Triton, or kernel efficiency being limited by Triton implementation.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss open-source model releases motivating inference-engine developers to add support.

r004.rationale: It says better systems support would let companies try these architectures without rewriting their serving stacks, lowering engineering cost and slowing adoption less.

astra-6.text:
I think the main bottleneck is translating the theoretical efficiency of linear attention into practical speed on hardware. Removing the quadratic attention matrix is attractive, but it doesn’t automatically make the model faster. You have to account for memory movement, how much of the computation can run in parallel, and how efficiently the kernels use the GPU.

There’s also a quality constraint. The recurrent state compresses the history into a fixed-size representation, so the challenge is retaining the information the model needs, especially for precise retrieval over long contexts. If you need a much larger state to match the quality of standard attention, that eats into the efficiency advantage.

So I’d frame the bottleneck as achieving competitive quality and actual hardware efficiency at the same time. Linear complexity alone isn’t enough; you need a model that trains efficiently and delivers better latency or throughput at the quality people need.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main bottleneck is turning the theoretical efficiency into practical efficiency while maintaining model quality. Linear attention avoids the quadratic attention matrix, but that doesn’t automatically make it faster on a GPU. The way you organize the computation, move data through memory, and parallelize training matters a lot.

There’s also a modeling tradeoff. You’re compressing the history into a fixed-size state, so you need to preserve the information that matters, especially for tasks that require recalling specific details from a long context. Making that state more expressive can increase the computational cost.

So I’d frame the challenge as co-designing the architecture and the implementation: getting competitive quality at scale, with kernels that translate the algorithmic savings into real improvements in training and inference.
